questions.q: Which of these is a statistical question?
o: How many hours do Class 7 students in our school sleep on a school night?
How many hours are there in one day?
At what time does our school assembly begin?
How many sides does a hexagon have?
questions.a: How many hours do Class 7 students in our school sleep on a school night? Different students sleep for different times, so data must be collected to answer it.

questions.q: Which of these is a statistical statement?
o: About 3 out of every 4 students in our class walk to school.
Our school gate is painted green.
Rahul walked to school this morning.
Do most students in our class walk to school?
questions.a: About 3 out of every 4 students in our class walk to school. It summarises data about many students using a proportion.

questions.q: Match each item in Column I with what it is in Column II. Column I: 1. 'How many legs does an ant have?'  2. 'How many minutes do children in our colony play outdoors each day?'  3. 'On average, a child in our colony plays outdoors for 50 minutes a day.'  4. Collecting, organising, analysing, interpreting and presenting data. Column II: a. A statistical statement  b. Not a statistical question  c. Statistics  d. A statistical question
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c: an ant's legs have one fixed answer; outdoor play time varies and needs data; the average is a summary of data; and statistics is the study of collecting, organising, analysing, interpreting and presenting data.

questions.q: True or False: 'What is the length of the blackboard in our classroom?' is a statistical question. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. The blackboard has one fixed length, so a single measurement answers it. A statistical question expects answers that vary and is answered by collecting data.
s: Reason: the question has one fixed answer, while a statistical question expects varied answers and needs data to be collected

questions.q: (a) What is a statistical question? (b) Give one example of a statistical question about the students of your school.
questions.a: (a) A statistical question is one that is answered by collecting data, because its answer is expected to vary. (b) For example, 'How long do the students of our school take to reach school in the morning?'
s: (a) A question answered by collecting data whose values are expected to vary
(b) A correct example about the school whose answer varies from student to student

questions.q: Assertion (A): 'How much does a 1-litre packet of milk cost at the dairy booth near my house today?' is not a statistical question, but 'How much does a 1-litre packet of milk cost in the shops of our town?' is a statistical question. Reason (R): A statistical question expects answers that vary, so it can be answered only by collecting and analysing data.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. One booth on one day has a single price, but prices across the town's shops vary, so data must be collected.

questions.q: Tanvi asks two questions: (i) 'How long did I take to walk to school today?' (ii) 'How long do I usually take to walk to school?' Arjun says, 'Neither is a statistical question, because both are about only one person.' Is Arjun right? Explain, and say what data Tanvi should collect to answer the statistical one.
questions.a: Arjun is only partly right. Question (i) is not statistical: one walk today has one time. Question (ii) is statistical even though it is about one person, because her walking time varies from day to day, like the book's 'I take about 15 minutes to cycle from school to home'. Tanvi should time her walk on many days and then summarise the times, for example with their average.
s: Verdict: Arjun is right about (i) but wrong about (ii)
Reason: one person's walking time varies from day to day, so (ii) needs data while (i) has one answer
Data plan: time the walk on several days and summarise, for example by the average

questions.q: The eco club of a school in Bhopal wants to study how much water the families of a housing society use. (a) Ravi's first question was 'How many buckets of water did my family use yesterday?' Explain why this is not a statistical question, and rewrite it as a statistical question. (b) The club recorded the buckets of water used in one day by 6 families: 9, 14, 7, 11, 16 and 9. Find the mean number of buckets per family. (c) Write one statistical statement from this data that uses a number. (d) A member says, 'So every family in the society uses 11 buckets a day.' Give two reasons why this is not justified.
questions.a: (a) It asks about one family on one day, so it has a single answer; a statistical version is 'How many buckets of water do the families of our society use in a day?' (b) Total = 9 + 14 + 7 + 11 + 16 + 9 = 66; mean = 66 / 6 = 11 buckets. (c) For example, 'On average, a family in our sample used 11 buckets of water in a day', or 'Half of the 6 families used more than 10 buckets.' (d) The mean is a fair-share value, and no family is shown to use exactly 11 (the values range from 7 to 16); also only 6 families on one day were studied, which cannot be generalised to every family on every day.
s: (a) Says it has one fixed answer and rewrites it as a question about many families
(c) A correct statistical statement using a number from the data
(d) Reason 1: the mean does not describe each family, since the values vary from 7 to 16
(d) Reason 2: 6 families on one day are too few to generalise to the whole society

questions.q: Gauri counts the pages she reads each day for five days: 12, 18, 9, 14 and 22. What is the mean number of pages she reads in a day?
o: 15 pages
75 pages
14 pages
13 pages
questions.a: 15 pages, because the total 75 divided by the 5 days is 15.

questions.q: Four friends pick 7, 3, 6 and 4 jamuns. They put all the jamuns together and share them equally. How many jamuns does each friend get?
o: 5 jamuns
20 jamuns
4 jamuns
7 jamuns
questions.a: 5 jamuns: the 20 jamuns shared equally among 4 friends gives each 5, which is the mean (fair share).

questions.q: In a quiz league, Team Neel (4 players) scored 92 points and Team Lal (5 players) scored 105 points. Each team shares its points equally among its own players. Which statement is correct?
o: Each Neel player's share is 23, which is 2 more than each Lal player's share of 21.
Team Lal did better per player, because its total of 105 is more than 92.
Each Lal player's share is 26.25, which is more than each Neel player's 18.4.
The teams cannot be compared at all, because they have different numbers of players.
questions.a: Each Neel player's share is 23 (92 / 4), which is 2 more than each Lal player's share of 21 (105 / 5). With different group sizes, the mean, not the total, is compared.

questions.q: Consider these statements. I. The mean of 4, 8, 6 and 10 is 28. II. The mean of a set of values need not be one of the values; for example, the mean of 2, 7, 9, 4 and 3 is 5. III. The ancient Indian term samamiti (mean measure) shows that the arithmetic mean was seen as an equalising value. Which of these are correct?
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I gives the total, 28; the mean is 28 / 4 = 7. Statement II is right, since 5 is not in the list, and Statement III matches the book's account of samamiti ('sama' means equal).

questions.q: Five sections of Class 7 collected 45, 52, 38, 49 and 41 kg of old newspaper for recycling. (a) Find the total collected. (b) Find the mean amount collected per section.
A milk booth sold 120, 135, 128, 142, 130 and 125 litres of milk on six days. (a) Find the total milk sold. (b) Find the mean sale per day. (c) On how many days was the sale more than the mean?
questions.a: (a) Total = 780 litres. (b) Mean = 780 / 6 = 130 litres per day. (c) On 2 days (135 and 142 litres); the day with 130 litres equals the mean.
s: (c) 2 days (135 and 142) are above the mean

questions.q: Ira and Maya counted how many times each could skip without a break on five days. Ira: 42, 38, 45, 40, 35. Maya: 30, 52, 44, 39, 45. (a) Find Ira's total. (b) Find Ira's mean. (c) Find Maya's total. (d) Find Maya's mean. (e) Who skipped more on average, and by how many skips?
questions.a: (a) Ira's total = 200. (b) Ira's mean = 200 / 5 = 40. (c) Maya's total = 210. (d) Maya's mean = 210 / 5 = 42. (e) Maya skipped more on average, by 42 - 40 = 2 skips.

questions.q: Two self-help groups in a village in Odisha make leaf plates. Group Sabuja has 5 members, who made 120, 95, 140, 110 and 135 plates in a week. Group Champa has 6 members, who made 100, 125, 90, 115, 105 and 125 plates in the same week. Each group is paid Rs 2 for every plate and shares its money equally among its own members. A buyer wants to give a bonus order to the group whose members make more plates on average. (a) Find the total number of plates made by each group. (b) Find the mean number of plates per member for each group. (c) How much money does each member of Sabuja get for the week? (d) Which group should get the bonus order? Justify, and say why comparing the totals would mislead the buyer.
questions.a: (a) Sabuja 600 plates, Champa 660 plates. (b) Sabuja 600 / 5 = 120; Champa 660 / 6 = 110 plates per member. (c) Sabuja earns 600 x 2 = Rs 1200, so each member gets 1200 / 5 = Rs 240. (d) Sabuja, because its members make 10 more plates each on average. Champa's total is larger only because it has one more member; with groups of different sizes, the mean is the fair comparison.
s: (d) Sabuja, since its mean is higher; the totals mislead because the groups differ in size

questions.q: In a reading drive, the 30 students of Section Tulip read a mean of 12 books each in a year, and the 20 students of Section Lotus read a mean of 17 books each. (a) How many books did Section Tulip read in all? (b) How many books did Section Lotus read in all? (c) Find the mean number of books per student for the two sections taken together. (d) Rohit says the combined mean is (12 + 17) / 2 = 14.5. Explain why he is wrong.
questions.a: (a) 30 x 12 = 360 books. (b) 20 x 17 = 340 books. (c) (360 + 340) / 50 = 700 / 50 = 14 books per student. (d) Rohit gives both sections equal weight, but Tulip has more students; the combined mean must be total books divided by total students, which is 14, not 14.5.
s: (d) Averaging the two means ignores the different section sizes

questions.q: The highest temperatures in Shimla on seven days of a week were 18, 22, 15, 20, 24, 17 and 19 degrees Celsius. What is the range of these temperatures?
o: 9 degrees Celsius
135 degrees Celsius
24 degrees Celsius
6 degrees Celsius
questions.a: 9 degrees Celsius: range = maximum - minimum = 24 - 15 = 9.

questions.q: Which of these best describes a dot plot?
o: Each value is shown as a dot above a number line, so clusters and spread are easy to see.
The values are shown in the order they were collected, one month after another.
Only the mean of the data is marked, as a single dot on a line.
Only the highest and lowest values are shown, joined by a straight line.
questions.a: In a dot plot each value is a dot above a number line, so we can see where the data clusters or spreads out (though the original order is lost).

questions.q: A dot plot shows a batter's runs in 10 innings. The stacks are: 5 (1 dot), 12 (2 dots), 20 (3 dots), 25 (1 dot), 31 (2 dots) and 64 (1 dot). Which statement is correct?
o: She scored 20 or more runs in 7 of the 10 innings.
The range of her scores is 64 - 12 = 52 runs.
She scored 20 runs in her third innings.
Most of her scores lie between 31 and 64 runs.
questions.a: She scored 20 or more runs in 7 of the 10 innings (3 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7 dots). The range is 64 - 5 = 59, and a dot plot does not show the order of the innings.

questions.q: Assertion (A): For the scores 35, 60, 48 and 52, the range is 13. Reason (R): Range = maximum value - minimum value.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. Using R, the range is 60 - 35 = 25, not 13.

questions.q: A fruit seller weighed six watermelons: 4.5, 6.2, 3.8, 5.0, 7.1 and 5.4 kg. (a) Write the minimum and the maximum weight. (b) Find the range.
questions.a: (a) Minimum 3.8 kg, maximum 7.1 kg. (b) Range = 7.1 - 3.8 = 3.3 kg.

questions.q: True or False: Adding a new score of 50 to the scores 42, 47, 55 and 39 does not change the range. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The range before is 55 - 39 = 16. The new score 50 lies between the minimum 39 and the maximum 55, so the range stays 55 - 39 = 16.
s: Reason: 50 lies between 39 and 55, so the maximum and minimum and the range 16 do not change

questions.q: Two bakeries sold these numbers of cakes on the same six days. Sweet Spot: 40, 85, 120, 210, 160, 95. Fresh Crust: 60, 70, 150, 190, 180, 70. Isha says, 'Sweet Spot sold more cakes over these days, because it had the highest sale on a single day, 210.' (a) Find each bakery's total. (b) Find each bakery's range. (c) Is Isha right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Sweet Spot 710, Fresh Crust 720. (b) Sweet Spot 210 - 40 = 170; Fresh Crust 190 - 60 = 130. (c) No. Fresh Crust sold 10 more cakes over the same six days. Sweet Spot's one high day only shows that its sales were more spread out (a larger range), not that it sold more.
s: (c) Isha is wrong: one highest value does not decide which sold more; the totals over the same days show Fresh Crust sold more

questions.q: The sports teacher of a school in Guwahati recorded how many push-ups 8 students did in one minute: 22, 18, 25, 30, 18, 27, 22 and 18. She plans to show the data as a dot plot on a number line marked from 15 to 30, with one dot for each student. (a) What is the maximum number of push-ups? (b) Find the range. (c) How many dots will be stacked above 18 on the dot plot? (d) Find the mean number of push-ups.
questions.a: (a) 30 push-ups. (b) Range = 30 - 18 = 12. (c) 3 dots, because three students did 18. (d) Mean = 180 / 8 = 22.5 push-ups.

questions.q: A coach must pick one of two archers for a match. Their scores (out of 10) in six practice rounds were: Diya 7, 8, 7, 9, 8, 9 and Esha 10, 4, 10, 5, 10, 9. (a) Find each archer's total. (b) Find each archer's mean. (c) Find each archer's range. (d) In this match a single poor round loses the match. Which archer should the coach pick? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Diya 48, Esha 48. (b) Both means are 48 / 6 = 8. (c) Diya 9 - 7 = 2; Esha 10 - 4 = 6. (d) Diya. Both have the same mean, so the mean cannot decide; Diya's smaller range shows she is more consistent, and Esha's 4 and 5 show she can have the poor round that loses the match.
s: (d) Picks Diya: equal means, so the smaller range (more consistent) decides

questions.q: What is the median of 13, 7, 21, 9 and 16?
questions.a: 13: sorted, the values are 7, 9, 13, 16, 21 and the middle one is 13.

questions.q: The heights of six sunflower plants are 92, 85, 101, 88, 96 and 90 cm. What is their median height?
o: 91 cm
90 cm
182 cm
questions.a: 91 cm: sorted, the heights are 85, 88, 90, 92, 96, 101; with an even number of values, the median is (90 + 92) / 2 = 91.

questions.q: Match each list in Column I with its median in Column II. Column I: 1. 3, 9, 5  2. 2, 8, 4, 10  3. 10, 1, 7, 4, 12  4. 15, 11, 20, 14. Column II: a. 6  b. 14.5  c. 5  d. 7
Seven children took these times (in minutes) to finish a 2 km fun run: 11, 12, 10, 13, 12, 11 and 33. Which statement is correct?
o: 33 is an outlier, and it pulls the mean above the median of 12.
33 is an outlier, and it pulls the median above the mean.
There is no outlier, since the mean and the median are both 12.
10 is the outlier, because it is the smallest value.
questions.a: 33 is an outlier, and it pulls the mean (102 / 7, about 14.57) above the median of 12.

questions.q: Seven students scored these marks (out of 20) in a spelling test: 15, 17, 4, 16, 18, 14, 17. (a) Which mark is an outlier? (b) Find the median mark.
questions.a: (a) 4, because it is far below all the other marks. (b) Sorted: 4, 14, 15, 16, 17, 17, 18; the median is 16.

questions.q: (a) What is the median of a set of data? (b) What is an outlier? (c) The heights of five plants are 140, 142, 145, 147 and 190 cm, and the median is 145 cm. If the 190 cm plant is replaced by one of 150 cm, does the median change? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) The median is the middle value when the data is sorted (or the average of the two middle values when there is an even number of values). (b) An outlier is a value that differs greatly from the rest of the data. (c) No. Sorted, the data becomes 140, 142, 145, 147, 150, and the middle value is still 145.
s: (a) Middle value of the sorted data
(b) A value far away from the rest of the data
(c) No: the middle value of the sorted data is still 145

questions.q: The ages of five children in a group are 6, 8, 9, 11 and 12 years. Ravi says, 'If one more child of the right age joins, I can make the median age 15.' Show that this is impossible.
questions.a: With 6 children, the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th ages after sorting. Even if the new child is very old, the sorted list is 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, (new), so the middle two are 9 and 11 and the median is (9 + 11) / 2 = 10. A younger new child only lowers it (down to 8.5). So the median can be at most 10, never 15.
s: With 6 values, the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th sorted values
A very old new child goes to the end, so the middle two are 9 and 11, giving 10
So the median is at most 10 and cannot be 15

questions.q: Eight children noted how many hours of TV they watched in a week: 6, 8, 5, 7, 9, 6, 7 and 40. (a) Find the mean. (b) Find the median. (c) Name the outlier, and find the mean without it (to two decimal places). (d) Which measure, the mean of all eight or the median, better describes the TV time of a typical child here? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Mean = 88 / 8 = 11 hours. (b) Sorted: 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 40; median = (7 + 7) / 2 = 7 hours. (c) The outlier is 40; without it the mean is 48 / 7, about 6.86 hours. (d) The median. The mean of 11 is more than seven of the eight values because the outlier 40 pulls it up, while the median 7 stays close to most children's times.
s: (c) Outlier 40; mean without it about 6.86 hours
(d) Median, because the high outlier pulls the mean above most values

questions.q: At a picnic, two groups noted their ages in years. Group Hills: 34, 36, 38, 35, 37. Group River: 8, 40, 42, 39, 41, 44. (a) Find the mean age of Group Hills. (b) Find the mean age of Group River, to two decimal places. (c) Find the median age of each group. (d) Which value is an outlier, and how does it affect Group River's mean? (e) Which group would you call older? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 180 / 5 = 36 years. (b) 214 / 6, about 35.67 years. (c) Hills: 36 years; River (sorted 8, 39, 40, 41, 42, 44): (40 + 41) / 2 = 40.5 years. (d) The 8-year-old child is an outlier at the lower end; it pulls River's mean down below its median (without it, River's mean would be 41.2). (e) Group River, because five of its six members are older than everyone in Group Hills, and its median (40.5) is higher; the mean alone makes River look younger only because of the one child.
s: (d) 8 is a low outlier that pulls River's mean down
(e) River is older, judged by the median and by most members, not by the mean

questions.q: Priya's scores in five class quizzes are 8, 0, 6, absent and 10. She took the second quiz and scored 0, but she was absent for the fourth. To find her mean score per quiz, the total 24 should be divided by which number?
o: By 4, because she took four quizzes and the 0 is a real score.
By 5, because every quiz in the list must be counted.
By 3, because both the 0 and the absent quiz are left out.
By 4, because the 0 is left out and the absent quiz is counted.
questions.a: By 4, because she took four quizzes and the 0 is a real score; the quiz she missed has no value and is not counted. Her mean is 24 / 4 = 6.

questions.q: Assertion (A): For the data 32, 35, 33, 36 and 2, the mean is less than the median. Reason (R): An outlier at the lower end pulls the median down more than it pulls the mean down.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. The mean is 138 / 5 = 27.6 and the median is 33, so A is true; but it is the mean, not the median, that the low outlier 2 pulls down.

questions.q: Consider these statements. I. When data has no outlier, the mean and the median are usually close to each other. II. When there is an outlier at the higher end, the mean is usually less than the median. III. If a player did not play a match, that match is not counted when her mean runs per match are found. Which of these are correct?
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: a high outlier pulls the mean up, so the mean is usually greater than the median.

questions.q: True or False: A shop was open all day on Tuesday but sold nothing, so its sale that day was Rs 0. This day must be counted when the mean daily sale of the week is found. Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The shop was open, so Rs 0 is a real value of the data and is counted. Only a day with no value at all, such as a day the shop was closed, is left out.
s: Reason: a zero is a real value and is counted; only a missing value (no data) is left out

questions.q: A kabaddi raider's points in six matches were 7, 0, 12, did not play, 9 and 2. (a) Find her mean points per match. (b) Find the median, and say why the mean is less than the median.
questions.a: (a) She played 5 matches: total 30, mean 30 / 5 = 6 points. (b) Sorted: 0, 2, 7, 9, 12, so the median is 7. The mean is less because the low values 0 and 2 pull it down.
s: (b) Median 7; the low values pull the mean below the median

questions.q: Sanya looks at the data 3, 48, 50, 49, 51 and 97 and says, 'This data has an outlier at each end, so the mean must be far away from the median.' (a) Find the mean, to two decimal places. (b) Find the median. (c) Is Sanya right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Mean = 298 / 6, about 49.67. (b) Sorted: 3, 48, 49, 50, 51, 97; median = (49 + 50) / 2 = 49.5. (c) No. The low outlier 3 pulls the mean down and the high outlier 97 pulls it up by about the same amount, so the two effects nearly cancel and the mean stays close to the median.
s: (c) Not right: outliers on both sides pull the mean in opposite directions, so mean and median stay close

questions.q: A school library records the books borrowed from Monday to Saturday: Monday 24, Tuesday 0 (the library was open, but no one borrowed during exams), Wednesday 18, Thursday closed for a holiday, Friday 30 and Saturday 28. (a) On how many days should the data be counted? (b) Find the total number of books borrowed. (c) Find the mean number of books borrowed per day. (d) Find the median.
questions.a: (a) 5 days: Tuesday's 0 is counted because the library was open, but Thursday has no value. (b) 24 + 0 + 18 + 30 + 28 = 100 books. (c) Mean = 100 / 5 = 20 books. (d) Sorted: 0, 18, 24, 28, 30; median = 24 books.
s: (a) 5 days: the 0 is counted, the closed day is not

questions.q: Rekha runs a juice stall near a college in Pune. She sold these numbers of glasses on 8 days: 48, 52, 50, 0, 55, 49, 51 and 175. On the day with 0, the stall was open but there was a power cut all day. The 175 was on the day of the college fest. Rekha wants one number for a typical day so that she can plan how much fruit to buy. (a) Find the mean number of glasses sold per day. (b) Find the median. (c) Which values are outliers, and at which ends of the data are they? (d) Should Rekha plan with the mean or the median? Justify, and say whether the 0 should be kept in the data.
questions.a: (a) 480 / 8 = 60 glasses. (b) Sorted: 0, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 55, 175; median = (50 + 51) / 2 = 50.5 glasses. (c) 0 is a low outlier and 175 is a high outlier. (d) The median: the mean of 60 is above 7 of the 8 days because 175 pulls it up more than 0 pulls it down, while the median 50.5 matches a normal day (the six normal days average about 50.83). The 0 is a real value, since the stall was open, so it stays in the data; the median is hardly affected by it.
s: (c) 0 is a low outlier and 175 a high outlier
(d) Median for planning, since the mean is above most days; the 0 is a real value and is kept

questions.q: A double bar graph uses the scale 1 unit = 10 students. How long is the bar for 65 students?
o: 6.5 units
65 units
650 units
0.65 units
questions.a: 6.5 units, because 65 / 10 = 6.5.

questions.q: A double bar graph shows library books borrowed by boys and girls in four months, with 1 unit = 8 books. The girls' bars are 3, 4.5, 5 and 2.5 units long, and the boys' bars are 3.5, 4, 5.5 and 2 units long. Which statement is correct?
o: Girls borrowed more in 2 of the 4 months, yet each group borrowed 120 books in all.
Girls borrowed more in 2 of the 4 months, so girls borrowed 8 more books in all.
Boys borrowed more books in all, because their longest bar, 5.5 units, is the longest.
Each group borrowed only 15 books in all over the four months.
questions.a: Girls borrowed more in 2 of the 4 months (4.5 > 4 and 2.5 > 2), yet both groups' bars add to 15 units, which is 15 x 8 = 120 books each.

questions.q: Match each feature of a double bar graph in Column I with its purpose in Column II. Column I: 1. Different colours or patterns for the two groups  2. A scale such as 1 unit = 5 hours  3. Months placed in order from January to December  4. Dots and slanted lines drawn inside the bars. Column II: a. Tells how much each unit of bar length stands for  b. Shows how the values change over time  c. Separates the two groups being compared  d. Helps readers who find it hard to tell colours apart, or who have a black-and-white print
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d: colours separate the two groups, the scale gives the value of one unit, ordered months show change over time, and patterns inside bars help readers who cannot tell colours apart or who use a black-and-white print.

questions.q: Assertion (A): In a double bar graph of monthly onion prices, the months are kept in order from January to December. Reason (R): On one graph, each unit of bar length stands for the same value.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The months are kept in order so that we can see how prices change over time; the equal scale is a different fact about bar graphs.

questions.q: A double bar graph of milk collected by two dairies uses the scale 1 unit = 6 litres. (a) How long is the bar for 45 litres? (b) How many litres does a bar of 4.5 units show?
questions.a: (a) 45 / 6 = 7.5 units. (b) 4.5 x 6 = 27 litres.

questions.q: A double bar graph shows the bottles of mango juice and orange juice sold by a shop in three weeks, with 1 unit = 12 bottles. Mango bars: 5, 6.5 and 8 units. Orange bars: 7, 6 and 4.5 units. (a) In which week did orange juice sell more than mango juice, and by how many bottles? (b) How many bottles of mango juice were sold in the three weeks?
questions.a: (a) Week 1: orange 7 units against mango 5 units, a difference of 2 units = 2 x 12 = 24 bottles. (b) Mango: 5 + 6.5 + 8 = 19.5 units = 19.5 x 12 = 234 bottles.

questions.q: Students of two classes chose clubs. Class 6: Art 18, Music 12, Sports 24. Class 7: Art 15, Music 21, Sports 27. A double bar graph is drawn with 1 unit = 3 students. (a) Find the bar lengths for Class 6. (b) Find the bar lengths for Class 7. (c) For which club are the two bars most different, and by how many students?
questions.a: (a) Class 6: Art 6, Music 4, Sports 8 units. (b) Class 7: Art 5, Music 7, Sports 9 units. (c) Music: 21 - 12 = 9 students (3 units); the other clubs differ by only 3 students.

questions.q: A double bar graph shows the number of late trains at two stations, P and Q, in four months, with 1 unit = 10 trains. Station P's bars are 4.5, 3, 6 and 2.5 units long; Station Q's bars are 3.5, 5, 4.5 and 4 units long (months 1 to 4). (a) What does Station P's first bar of 4.5 units stand for? (b) Find the total number of late trains at each station. (c) In which month is the gap between the stations largest, and how large is it? (d) Find the mean number of late trains per month at each station. (e) A reporter writes, 'Station P is always worse than Station Q.' Is this justified? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 4.5 x 10 = 45 late trains at P in month 1. (b) P: 45 + 30 + 60 + 25 = 160; Q: 35 + 50 + 45 + 40 = 170. (c) Month 2: Q had 50 and P had 30, a gap of 20 trains. (d) P: 160 / 4 = 40; Q: 170 / 4 = 42.5 trains per month. (e) No. P had more late trains only in months 1 and 3; Q had more in months 2 and 4 and has the higher total and mean.
s: (e) Not justified: P is worse only in two months and has the lower total and mean

questions.q: A district office in Karnataka drew a double bar graph of the solar water pumps installed by farmers in two taluks in 2022, 2023 and 2024. The scale is 1 unit = 50 pumps. Taluk Arali's bars are 2, 5 and 8 units long; Taluk Bevu's bars are 6, 6.5 and 7 units long. The office will open one new training centre for pump repair in the taluk where installations are growing fastest. (a) How many pumps were installed in Arali in 2024? (b) By how many pumps did Bevu's installations increase from 2022 to 2024? (c) How many times did Arali's installations grow from 2022 to 2024? (d) Bevu installed more pumps over the three years. Which taluk should get the training centre? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) 8 x 50 = 400 pumps. (b) Bevu: 300 in 2022 and 350 in 2024, an increase of 50 pumps. (c) Arali: 100 in 2022 to 400 in 2024, so 4 times. (d) Arali. Bevu's three-year total is larger (975 against 750), but the centre is meant for the fastest growth, and Arali grew by 300 pumps (4 times) while Bevu grew by only 50.
s: (d) Arali, because it is growing much faster, even though Bevu's total is larger

questions.q: A national survey table gives the average height of 8-year-old boys in India as 120.9 cm in 2009 and 123.5 cm in 2019. By how much did this average height rise?
o: 2.6 cm
3.6 cm
1.6 cm

questions.q: A survey table gives the average heights of 17-year-olds in India in 2019: boys 164.6 cm and girls 154.7 cm. (a) Who was taller on average? (b) By how much?

A survey table gives these average heights (cm) of 16-year-olds in India. Boys: 158.9 in 1989, 158.7 in 1999, 162.3 in 2019. Girls: 150.1 in 1989, 150.1 in 1999, 153.8 in 2019. Which statement CAN be justified by this data?
o: The average height of 16-year-old girls was the same in 1989 and 1999.
The average height of 16-year-old boys rose in every decade from 1989 to 2019.
Every 16-year-old boy in 2019 was taller than every 16-year-old girl.
In 2029 the average 16-year-old boy will be 165.9 cm tall.
questions.a: The average height of 16-year-old girls was the same in 1989 and 1999 (150.1 cm both times). The boys' average fell slightly from 158.9 to 158.7, averages say nothing about every individual, and the table cannot fix a 2029 value.

questions.q: A survey table gives these average heights (cm) in India. Age 7 girls: 111.4 in 1989, 118.0 in 2019. Age 9 in 2019: boys 128.1, girls 127.6. Age 18 boys: 162.9 in 1989, 166.0 in 2019. Consider these statements. I. From 1989 to 2019, the average height of 7-year-old girls rose by 6.6 cm. II. In 2019, the average 9-year-old girl was taller than the average 9-year-old boy. III. From 1989 to 2019, the average height of 18-year-old boys rose by 4.1 cm. Which of these are correct?
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
questions.a: I only. 118.0 - 111.4 = 6.6, so Statement I is right; in 2019 the 9-year-old girls' average (127.6) was below the boys' (128.1); and 166.0 - 162.9 = 3.1, not 4.1.

questions.q: A survey table gives the average heights (cm) of girls in India in 2019: age 7: 118.0, age 8: 122.7, age 9: 127.6, age 16: 153.8, age 17: 154.7, age 18: 155.2. (a) Find how much the average height increases from age 7 to 8 and from age 8 to 9. (b) Find how much it increases from age 16 to 17 and from age 17 to 18. (c) What story do these numbers tell about how girls grow?
questions.a: (a) 122.7 - 118.0 = 4.7 cm and 127.6 - 122.7 = 4.9 cm. (b) 154.7 - 153.8 = 0.9 cm and 155.2 - 154.7 = 0.5 cm. (c) Girls grow by nearly 5 cm a year at ages 7 to 9, but by less than 1 cm a year at ages 16 to 18, so their growth slows down greatly in the late teens.
s: (c) Growth is fast at 7 to 9 and almost stops by 16 to 18

questions.q: A survey table gives these 2019 average heights (cm) in India. Age 8: boys 123.5, girls 122.7. Age 11: boys 137.0, girls 138.6. Kunal says, 'The table shows that boys are taller than girls at every age, so my 8-year-old cousin sister must be shorter than my 8-year-old brother.' (a) Is the first part of his claim justified by these values? (b) Can these averages decide whether his sister is shorter than his brother? (c) Write one statement about these four values that is justified.
questions.a: (a) No. At age 11 the girls' average (138.6) is more than the boys' (137.0). (b) No. An average describes the group as a whole, not each child, so a higher boys' average does not mean every boy is taller than every girl; the two children must be measured. (c) For example, 'In 2019 the average 8-year-old boy was 0.8 cm taller than the average 8-year-old girl.'
s: (a) Not justified: at age 11 the girls' average is higher
(b) Averages do not decide about two particular children
(c) A correct statement such as: 8-year-old boys were 0.8 cm taller on average in 2019

questions.q: A survey table gives the average height (cm) of 9-year-old boys in India as 122.9 in 1989, 123.9 in 1999, 125.2 in 2009 and 128.1 in 2019. For 9-year-old girls it gives 121.7 in 1989 and 127.6 in 2019. (a) Find the rise in the boys' average in each decade. (b) In which decade was the rise greatest? (c) Find the total rise for boys from 1989 to 2019. (d) Find the mean rise per decade for boys, to two decimal places. (e) Did boys or girls gain more height on average from 1989 to 2019, and by how much?
questions.a: (a) 1989 to 1999: 1.0 cm; 1999 to 2009: 1.3 cm; 2009 to 2019: 2.9 cm. (b) 2009 to 2019. (c) 128.1 - 122.9 = 5.2 cm. (d) 5.2 / 3, about 1.73 cm per decade. (e) Girls gained 127.6 - 121.7 = 5.9 cm, which is 0.7 cm more than the boys' 5.2 cm.
s: (d) Mean rise about 1.73 cm per decade

questions.q: A school in Nagpur recorded the mean number of minutes its Class 7 students spent reading at home each day, for three sections and two terms. Term 1: Section A 22, Section B 30, Section C 18. Term 2: Section A 28, Section B 29, Section C 27. The principal wants to give an award to the section whose reading habit improved the most. (a) Find the change from Term 1 to Term 2 for each section. (b) Which section had the highest mean in Term 2? (c) Is the statement 'Every student of Section B read for 29 minutes a day in Term 2' justified? Why? (d) Section B's teacher says her section should get the award because it read the most in both terms. Which section should get the award? Justify.
questions.a: (a) A: +6 minutes, B: -1 minute, C: +9 minutes. (b) Section B, with 29 minutes. (c) No. 29 is a mean, a fair-share value; some students read more and some less. (d) Section C. The award is for improvement, and C improved by 9 minutes while B's mean actually fell by 1 minute; B's high level deserves praise, but it is not improvement.
s: (c) Not justified: a mean does not describe every student
(d) Section C, since the award is for improvement and C improved most
